title: What David Zaslav Got Wrong About ‘Coyote vs. Acme’
description: Three years after “Coyote vs. Acme” was shelved by Warner Bros. as a tax write-off and rescued by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment, the Loone
body:
Three years after “Coyote vs. Acme” was shelved by Warner Bros. as a tax write-off and rescued by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment, the Looney Tunes comedy has become a box-office bright spot with more than $100 million globally. Was Warner Bros. Discovery chief David Zaslav, who deemed it financially unworthy to release on the big screen, wrong to axe the film?

	That answer might depend on who is doing the accounting, analysts say. “Coyote vs. Acme” is a major win for Ketchup Entertainment, which paid $50 million for distribution rights and pre-sold foreign territories to offset the cost. Those grosses might not have been as celebratory for Warner Bros., considering the film cost $70 million to produce. (Theater owners get to keep half of ticket sales.) Warner Bros. dumped the live-action animation hybrid, starring Will Forte and John Cena and produced by DC Studios co-chief James Gunn, for a $30 million tax write-down.
	

	There’s an argument to be made that Warner Bros. would have been able to put more marketing dollars behind the release, which could have elevated global ticket sales. There’s another case that moviegoers rallied only behind “Coyote vs. Acme” to prove the studio wrong. By comparison, “Coyote vs. Acme” dramatically outperformed another recent Ketchup-distributed Looney Tunes adventure, 2024’s “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie,” after Warner Bros. Discovery quietly decided to offload that film as well. “The Day the Earth Blew Up,” whose target audience skewed much younger, grossed $15.4 million globally.
	

	“It’s easy to opine on a decision after we’ve seen the effects,” says Shawn Robbins, founder of Box Office Theory and director of movie analytics at Fandango. “The movie did well partly because of rallying from fans. But it turned out to be a good movie.”

	Buoyed by great reviews and positive word of mouth, “Coyote vs. Acme” launched in late August and started strong with $15.9 million domestically. Ticket sales have since climbed to $59.8 million domestically and $45 million overseas, underscoring the value of PG-rated films with brand familiarity. Theater owners frequently complain that they don’t have enough new movies aimed at families. And while original animation has struggled in post-COVID years, remakes, spinoffs and sequels in known franchises, such as “Sonic the Hedgehog” and “PAW Patrol,” have been reliable as modest box office draws.

	The success of “Coyote vs. Acme” is especially glaring given Warner Bros.’ abysmal 2026 box-office performance. The studio has siphoned off a string of money losers, including Tom Cruise’s dark comedy “Digger,” Maggie Gyllenhaal’s punk rock “The Bride!” and DC’s “Supergirl.”

	“There was legacy value in that IP, and the box office grosses of ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ reflect it,” says analyst David A. Gross of FranchiseRe. “All-audience films are extremely valuable and among the biggest earners at the box office. And there would have been upside with stronger marketing.”

	Moreover, the wall-to-wall negative press Zaslav generated for shelving a finished movie (that was supposedly well received in test screenings) wasn’t worth the headache, according to studio sources. The decision did little to endear the former television executive to the film community after his predecessor Jason Kilar’s ill-fated decision to put the studio’s 2021 slate simultaneously in theaters and on HBO Max had isolated many creatives in Hollywood. Although other employees within Warner Bros. pushed back on the decision to bury the film, Zaslav relegated the final call to accountants, sources add.

	At the time, “Coyote vs. Acme” was the third casualty of Zaslav’s post-pandemic cost-cutting efforts. In 2022, he shocked Hollywood by shelving the $90 million DC-centric “Batgirl” and kid-friendly “Scoob! Holiday Haunt” for tax purposes. Those three films were greenlit by Kilar, the studio’s former chief who departed earlier that year. Zaslav, who succeeded Kilar, said at the time he was shifting the studio’s priorities back to theatrical and felt “Coyote vs. Acme” didn’t fit with the new creative direction of the company. Box office watchers wonder whether Zaslav understood the value of the Warner Bros. catalog. After all, “Coyote vs. Acme,” “Batgirl” and “Scoob” hail from well-known brands. And there’s a reason that studios invest so heavily in recognizable franchises – they’re designed to turn the kind of easy profits that help justify other original swings.
	

	“We see so many remakes and sequels because they make money,” says Robbins. “The fact that ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ was based on IP plays into the curiosity behind Warner Bros. [getting rid of it].”

schema.headline: What David Zaslav Got Wrong About ‘Coyote vs. Acme’

title: Taylor Swift’s ‘Encore’ Edition Boosts ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ Back to No. 1 for First Time Since January, Adding a 13th Week on Top
description: Taylor Swift‘s “The Life of a Showgirl” returned to the No. 1 spot on the Billboard 200 album chart after last vacating that position in January, th
body:
Taylor Swift‘s “The Life of a Showgirl” returned to the No. 1 spot on the Billboard 200 album chart after last vacating that position in January, thanks to the release of an expanded edition titled “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore” with four new bonus tracks. This resumption at the top marks the 13th week the album has spent at No. 1, a lucky number Swift was surely looking to achieve all these months later.

	The deluxe edition collected 173,000 equivalent units in its first week — or in the 52nd week for all versions of the album, depending on how you’re looking at it. Most of that was from streaming consumption of the four new tracks, since Swift has not put any physical copies of the expanded set up for sale yet, so sales have been limited to a digital download. 
	

	Album sales accounted for 21,000 of the overall 173,000 total, with most of the rest coming from streaming, with SEA units adding up to 136,000 — that number representing 138.79 million on-demand official streams —  according to Billboard and Luminate.


	Swift’s new single, “Patient Zero,” is also expected to bow at No. 1 on the singles chart, Billboard’s Hot 100, but that chart’s top 10 won’t be released till Monday.

	The race to see who would come out on top among the week’s two other top 10 album bows was a squeaker, separated by a few hundred units. Tinashe’s “Popstar” enters at No. 6 with 35,500 equivalent album units. Kenny Chesney’s “Silver Sands Marina” is right behind it at No. 7 with 35,000. Chesney’s numbers for his new album ride the success of his “Carry On” single, which just became his record-extending 34th No. 1 song at country radio this past week.
	

	“The Life of a Showgirl” last had the No. 1 spot for the chart week ending Jan. 10, 2026. At that time, it was enjoying its 12th (and, at that point, seemingly final?) non-consecutive week on top of the Billboard 200, having prevailed from its October 2025 release through much of the Christmas buying season. Even before it added a 13th week with this return, “Showgirl” already had her second-highest number of weeks at No. 1. Her record for that is held by “The Tortured Poets Department,” which spent 17 weeks atop the chart. “1989” and “Fearless” are tied in her catalog with 11 weeks at No. 1 each. 

	Consumption for the expanded “Showgirl” was aided not just by the four new tracks but the release of a high-profile music video for “Patient Zero,” costarring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell, which premiered on the MTV Video Music Awards last Sunday night.

	Last week’s No. 1, Miley’s “Bass Persuades,” drops out of the top 10 this week. How far out of the top 10 was not revealed, as Billboard and Luminate only release the chart’s top 10 each Sunday and issue the rest of the top 200 albums in the days to follow. 

	Rounding out the top 10 albums are Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl in Love” at No. 2 (with 67,000 units), followed by long-players from Ella Langley at No. 3, Morgan Wallen at No. 4, Noah Kahan at No. 5 and Olivia Dean at No. 8. An earlier Kahan album, “Stick Season,” is at No. 9 and marks him as the only artist at present with two records in this upper echelon, while Drake closes out the top 10.

schema.headline: Taylor Swift’s ‘Encore’ Edition Boosts ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ Back to No. 1 for First Time Since January, Adding a 13th Week on Top

title: Gypsy-Rose Blanchard Launches Petition to ‘Fight Online Harassment’ Following Partner Ken Urker’s Death: ‘Fame Does Not Erase Humanity’
description: Gypsy-Rose Blanchard is speaking out following the death of her partner Ken Urker and urging fans to support Kenan’s Law, a petition aimed at holdin
body:
Gypsy-Rose Blanchard is speaking out following the death of her partner Ken Urker and urging fans to support Kenan’s Law, a petition aimed at holding social media platforms accountable for how online harassment is handled.

	While a cause of death has not yet been released, Blanchard wrote that before Urker passed, the two repeatedly reported harassment and cyberbullying he received across platforms including TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Reddit. She wrote that they believed such content “crossed the line from criticism.”
	

	“Ken was a public figure and experienced an enormous amount of public scrutiny,” she wrote. “Ken made reports. I made reports. Videos were reported. Comments were reported. Posts were reported. And many times, the answer we received was: ‘No violation.’ That is the problem I want to change.”

	Blanchard continued: “Being a public figure does not mean you stop being human. Public figures read the comments. They see the videos. They have children. They have parents. They have families. They experience the consequences of what happens online. Fame does not erase humanity.”

	Urker, who also fathered a baby girl, Aurora, with Blanchard, was found dead Thursday in Raceland, Louisiana. He was 34. Captain Brennan Matherne of the Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Department said in a statement to Variety, “We responded to a residence at 107 Double H Drive, Lot 4, in Raceland today after receiving a call at 6:15 p.m. Kenan Urker, 34, was found dead upon arrival. At this time, we are continuing the death investigation.”

	“Ken recently died following a suspected overdose,” Blanchard wrote in the petition. “At this time, we do not know whether the overdose was intentional, and I will not speculate about circumstances that have not been determined.”
	

	Urker appeared on the reality series “Gypsy Rose: Life After Lockup,” which ran for two seasons on Lifetime.

schema.headline: Gypsy-Rose Blanchard Launches Petition to ‘Fight Online Harassment’ Following Partner Ken Urker’s Death: ‘Fame Does Not Erase Humanity’

title: James Gunn Confirms He’s ‘Already’ Writing His Next Film Ahead of ‘Superman: Man of Tomorrow’
description: James Gunn announced on Threads that he is actively working on writing his next film ahead of the release of “Superman: Man of Tomorrow,” due in the
body:
James Gunn announced on Threads that he is actively working on writing his next film ahead of the release of “Superman: Man of Tomorrow,” due in theaters July 9, 2027. 

	In response to a comment that asked, “Are you ready to write your next film, James, or not quite yet?” Gunn wrote, “Already in it. I had to do something while I was waiting for the assembly!”

	Gunn also confirmed on the platform that the assembly cut of “Superman: Man of Tomorrow” is complete. In August, he’d previously confirmed that filming of the superhero flick had wrapped. 
	

	“Superman: Man of Tomorrow” is the sequel to 2025’s “Superman,” with David Corenswet returning as the Man of Steel. In the sequel, Superman is forced to team up with his adversary Lex Luthor (Nicholas Hoult) as they work to defeat an even bigger threat: the superintelligent antagonist Brainiac (Lars Eidinger).

	Rachel Brosnahan is back as Lois Lane. Other returning cast members include Skyler Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen, Sara Sampaio as Eve Teschmacher, Isabela Merced as Hawkgirl, Nathan Fillion as Guy Gardner and Edi Gathegi as Mister Terrific. Milly Alcock, who cameoed as Superman’s cousin Kara Zor-El, returns for “Man of Tomorrow” after headlining this summer’s DC tentpole, “Supergirl.” The sequel will also introduce Aaron Pierre to the big screen as John Stewart, who is debuting in the HBO Max series “Lanterns.”

	Along with writing and directing his “Superman” films, Gunn began running DC Studios alongside Peter Safran in 2022.

	“Peter’s the best,” Gunn told Variety in January. “He does everything I don’t do well. He keeps the ship steady, keeps everyone aligned, connects us with Jim Lee and the comics side and unifies departments that used to operate separately. What we share is a genuine love for these characters. We know what a privilege it is to help shape how people see them now — and that responsibility is something we take seriously.”

schema.headline: James Gunn Confirms He’s ‘Already’ Writing His Next Film Ahead of ‘Superman: Man of Tomorrow’

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Peacock subscribers were hit with another rate hike over the summer, with prices for the NBCUniversal streaming service rising for the fourth time in four years. The price hike came on the heels of Peacock dumping its free trial for new users, joining the ranks of rival streamers like Paramount+, Hulu and HBO Max, all of whom also got rid of their free trial offers.

	But there’s now a way to score a discount on Peacock, as well as take advantage of a free trial, though you’ll have to look elsewhere to claim the latter. Amazon is currently offering a 7-day free trial to Peacock through its Prime Channels hub.


	The deal gets you access to Peacock Premium Plus for free for one week if you sign up through Amazon. Premium Plus is the ad-free streaming tier of Peacock, and now costs $19.99/month (up from $16.99/month earlier this year).

	You won’t be able to find the free trial deal on the Peacock website. With the Prime Channels deal though, you can test drive the service for a week for free, with unlimited access to the entire on-demand library of TV shows and movies, as well as hundreds of hours of live sports streaming. 

	Though there isn’t a catch per se, the Peacock free trial offer is only open to Amazon Prime members (not a Prime member? Get a 30-day free trial here to claim the Peacock deal and get access to exclusive member discounts just in time for Prime Big Deal Days).

	Sign in with your Prime member details and then head to the Prime Video Channels homepage to claim the Peacock free trial offer. Your subscription to Peacock renews at the regular $19.99/month rate after your free trial is up. Or you can cancel at anytime to avoid being charged.

	
		What Are the Best Peacock Streaming Deals 2026?	

	In addition to the Premium Plus plan, Peacock’s latest rate increase brought the price of its Peacock Premium tier (which includes ads) to $12.99/month, up from $10.99/month previously. Its Peacock Select tier, meantime (which includes current and past seasons of select TV shows, but excludes movies, live sports and Peacock originals) jumped from $7.99 to $8.99/month. 

	Still, there’s a way to score a discount on a Peacock subscription. The streamer is offering an annual plan discount right now that gets you 12 months of access for the price of ten.

	The total price is $129 and locks in access for an entire year. That saves you 17% versus paying for Peacock month to month. The limited-time offer is available to all new and eligible returning subscribers and there is no promo code needed.

	Peacock has priced its annual subscription down to as low as $79.99 a year in the past, but with the streamer being home to the recent Olympics and Super Bowl this year, it was able to raise its prices to bring in audiences for the sporting events and it’s unlikely we’ll see a further discount from the current promotion live online.
	
		How to Get Peacock for Free	

	In addition to the Prime Channels free trial offer mentioned above, you can get Peacock for free with a Walmart+ membership. Walmart+ costs $98/year and as part of your membership, members can choose between Peacock Premium or Paramount+ Essential at no added cost.

	That’s in addition to perks like free shipping, free grocery delivery, special discounts, gas savings and more. Sign up for Walmart+ here (you can also test-drive the service for 30 day for just $1 here).

	You can also stream Peacock online for free with Instacart+. The grocery delivery service offers an upgraded tier that gets members free grocery delivery, free restaurant delivery and an annual membership to Peacock for free. Instacart+ costs just $9.99/month or $99/year. Try it out with a 14-day free trial here.

	Peacock is also home to hundreds of new movies such as “Obsession,” “F1” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” plus fan-favorite shows like “Pluribus,” “New Girl,” “The Traitors” “The Office” and the Bravo universe franchises.

	Peacock is also a top-choice streamer for sports fans, who can live stream live sports like the NFL, Premier League, Big Ten Football, and WWE.

title: Sass Jordan, Singer and Longtime ‘Canadian Idol’ Judge, Dies at 65
description:
Sass Jordan, the singer, songwriter and longtime “Canadian Idol” judge, died on Oct. 2. She was 65.

	Her family confirmed her death, noting that sh
body:
Sass Jordan, the singer, songwriter and longtime “Canadian Idol” judge, died on Oct. 2. She was 65.

	Her family confirmed her death, noting that she “died peacefully” and was “surrounded by those who loved her most.” They remembered her as “an inimitable force of nature” and “an irreplaceable being of light and joy.” 

	Jordan began her recording career in 1986 as co-lead vocalist on “Come On (Baby Tonight)” from Bündock’s album “Mauve.” She quickly became a sought-after session singer in Montreal, most notably on The Box’s breakthrough “L’Affaire Dumoutier (Say To Me…)”, and appeared in the band’s video for “Closer Together.”
	

	She was also a prominent songwriter. Michael Breen took her composition “Rain” onto the Canadian charts in 1987.


	In 1989, Jordan won the Juno Award for Most Promising Female Vocalist of the Year after her debut album, “Tell Somebody.”

	After moving to Los Angeles in Jan. 1990, she released “Racine” in March 1992. It became the defining album of her career, selling an estimated 450,000 copies worldwide and 100,000 in Canada on the strength of “Make You a Believer,” “I Want to Believe,” “You Don’t Have to Remind Me” and “Goin’ Back Again,” with “Who Do You Think You Are” following in 1993.

	“Make You a Believer” climbed to #11 on Billboard’s Mainstream Rock chart, and Billboard named her its top female rock artist of 1992.

	She joined “Canadian Idol” as a judge in 2003, the only woman on the panel, and stayed for all six seasons. She continued performing and releasing music for two decades.

	“If you love music and you’ve been around as long as I have, you pretty much do what you got to do,” Jordan once said. “But I love music. I am a huge, gigantic fan.”
	

	Born Sarah Jordan on Dec. 23, 1960, in Birmingham, England, she was the daughter of French literature professor Albert Jordan and former English ballerina Jean Lanceman. She began singing with friends at a young age and, by 16, was fronting bands in downtown Montreal clubs; later, she became singer and bassist for local favorites The Pinups.

	She is survived by her husband, Derek Sharp, daughter Stella Jordan-Sharp (Daniel Yepes), stepdaughter Brianne Sharp and brother Daniel Jordan (Isabelle Courville).

schema.headline: Sass Jordan, Singer and Longtime ‘Canadian Idol’ Judge, Dies at 65

title: ‘East of Eden’ Boss Zoe Kazan on That Devastating Ending, Why Florence Pugh’s Cathy Is Both a ‘Murderer’ and ‘Survivor’ and Making Lee a Central Character
description:
Oct 4, 2026 9:30am PT	
	

	
	‘East of Eden’ Boss Zoe Kazan on That Devastating Ending, Why Florence Pugh’s Cathy Is Both a ‘Murderer’ and ‘Sur
body:
Oct 4, 2026 9:30am PT	
	

	
	‘East of Eden’ Boss Zoe Kazan on That Devastating Ending, Why Florence Pugh’s Cathy Is Both a ‘Murderer’ and ‘Survivor’ and Making Lee a Central Character
	



			
			
	
						

									Courtesy of Netflix
	
					


							
		

	SPOILER ALERT: This interview contains major spoilers from “East of Eden,” now streaming on Netflix.

	Zoe Kazan has spent much of her life thinking about family legacy on and off screen. More than 62 years after her grandfather Elia Kazan famously directed James Dean in an adaptation of the fourth and final part of John Steinbeck’s novel “East of Eden,” the younger Kazan has taken on the Herculean task of tackling the full literary epic in a sweeping new Netflix miniseries, which premiered on Oct. 1.

	But rather than focusing strictly on the men of the Trask and Hamilton families, this adaptation shifts the spotlight to Cathy Ames (played by Florence Pugh, also an executive producer). Instead of being depicted merely as the amoral villain who shoots her husband Adam Trask (Christopher Abbott) and abandons her newborn twins to return to a life of prostitution, Cathy is reframed as a complex antihero whose choices ripple through generations of the Trask family.

	This shift also required trimming other major characters in this adaptation. Mike Faist, who plays Adam’s brother Charles, and Ciarán Hinds, who plays patriarch Samuel Hamilton, take on reduced roles compared to the novel. By tightening those subplots, the series focuses more by design on exploring the inner lives of Cathy, Adam and Lee (Hoon Lee) — the Trask’s cook and housekeeper who becomes a second parent of sorts to Charles’ twin boys, Cal and Aron.



	

									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	“Part of what the book is deeply about is: What do we do with the terrible things that have happened to us, or that we have done, or that have come before us?” Kazan tells Variety. “I was really interested in including Cathy in that narrative.”


	In the wide-ranging conversation below, Kazan opens up about using Steinbeck’s work to craft a distinctly personal take on “East of Eden,” fighting to expand the story of Lee despite budget constraints, and why she is relieved to bring far less familial baggage to her next adaptation of “Lonesome Dove.”

	
		In “East of Eden,” both you and Steinbeck grapple with a shared question of whether these men can escape the shadow of their family history and forge their own paths, or whether they are bound to that legacy. What intrigued you about telling this multi-generational — and ultimately tragic — love story between fathers, sons and brothers?	

	I read this book when I was 15, and I do ask myself: Did this book hit me hard because I was already thinking about these questions of what you carry from your family’s past, and what you do with that going forward? Or did I read this book and learn how to think about those things from it? This is one of the books that made me who I am. It’s not like my other work, but across a lot of my work, I’m thinking about families and the way people hurt each other by loving each other, or hurt each other in the name of love, and how terrible it is to be put in a box by someone’s conception of you and how you break out of that box.

	The reason for me to do this was to tell that intergenerational story. Cathy bounced off the page at me, but I don’t know that I would’ve raised my hand and been like, “I have to do this with six years of my life,” if it had just been for Cathy. We interviewed a lot of directors for this, and one female director I talked to really objected to me putting as much emphasis on the boys as I did. She was like, “If you were a real feminist, you would’ve made this whole thing about Cathy.”


	
		Wow.	

	It was a really clarifying meeting to have, because it made me understand even more deeply why these men’s stories speak to me so loudly, which is to say that I do not think of my own relationship to feminism as being a relationship that excludes men. I’m only interested in a version of gender parity that celebrates cis men, cis women, trans men, trans women, nonbinary people. I’m not interested in a small slice of humanity. The humanity of all of these characters — and getting to chart that over time and see how change happens, or doesn’t happen, in the family — is what drew me in.



	

					Ciarán Hinds 
									Courtesy of Netflix
	




	
		Steinbeck’s novel is largely centered around the Hamiltons (who emigrate from Ireland to the author’s beloved Salinas Valley) and the Trasks (who move to California from the East Coast). Why did you choose to cut down the Hamiltons’ storyline and center your adaptation instead around Cathy?	

	It became clear to me pretty early that if I was going to keep it at eight episodes or fewer, I was not going to have enough real estate for the Hamiltons. It was really important to me that this didn’t turn into a survey course of American history. I really wanted to go deep with these characters. A lot of the Hamilton stuff is quite emotional and deeply meaningful to the greater themes of the book. Tom Hamilton is probably my favorite character in the whole thing. But at a plot level, it’s really episodic. It doesn’t build in a dramatic narrative sense; it doesn’t go someplace the same way that the Trask storyline does. So by the time I got to the fifth episode, I knew that I was going to have to sacrifice that.

	There are novels that are all just poetry and emotion and themes, in which nothing happens. I think while an art film can do that, that’s not really what television is for. Even though I was trying to make something really timeless and that maybe stood out from the medium, I was also trying to make a piece of entertainment. One of the things that’s really important to me about the book is that it’s not “high art.” It was a piece of populist entertainment that he was writing, and I really wanted to preserve that.

	I know that we’ve talked in the press about this new emphasis on Cathy Ames. That was more in response to the 1965 film, which really sidelines her, than the actual book, which I think is fascinated by her. Cathy is the plot engine of this book. She is the troublemaker. She fascinated me from the start. I’m so curious about her — and I think Steinbeck was too — so I don’t see it as being quite as revisionist as maybe some of the articles have been framing my take as.



	

					Florence Pugh and Christopher Abbott 
									Courtesy of Netflix
	




	
		While Steinbeck explicitly frames Cathy as someone “born a monster” devoid of a moral soul, your adaptation reimagines her as an antihero driven by self-preservation and autonomy. How did you come to understand her underlying motivations, and what did you want this series to reveal about what truly makes her tick?	

	Even though I’ve never done any of the terrible things that Cathy does, reading this book for the first time, my identification was with Cathy. She’s unbelievably mysterious — and she’s not one thing. She is a liar, and she’s incredibly honest. She is a murderer, and she is a person who is trying to survive. There are things that Steinbeck describes in the book that I read slightly differently than he maybe intended them.

	Steinbeck posits that she, as a child, staged a rape with multiple little boys, and the description of that is incredibly upsetting. It says that she couldn’t speak afterwards — that when she did speak, no one believed her. It is impossible for me, as a person who grew up in a body that was sexualized and targeted from my earliest memories, not to read that as maybe not what Steinbeck intended. I think that there’s a ton of textual evidence for it. Very late in the book, she describes her memories of being a child and being frightened and alone, and how in those moments she would pretend that she was shrinking down with “Alice in Wonderland” and disappearing into Wonderland where nobody could hurt her. What I saw was a portrait of disassociation, and I profoundly understood that.


	
		The combination of your writing and Florence’s performance makes your interpretation of Cathy particularly hard to pin down, because she is so mercurial by nature, especially toward the final years of her life as this madam of a brothel. How did you think about scripting Cathy’s descent into madness?	

	Steinbeck kept a journal while he was writing this book. He wrote longhand on these big ledger books. He wrote his pages for the day on the right-hand side, and he would write letters to his friend and editor, Pascal Covici, on the left-hand side. Those letters were published, and I weirdly had read them already when I started adapting this, but I used those letters as a real North Star for me in understanding Steinbeck’s intentions. One of the things that’s really clear to me is that his viewpoint of her changed as he wrote. He goes from saying, “Oh, I’m going to write a monster unlike any you’ve ever seen,” to saying, “I think we all have a little monster blood in us, and people will hate her not because she is foreign, but because she is familiar.”

	I don’t have any proof for this, but I think he didn’t know what to do with that empathy. I think it surprised him — maybe it crept up on him. One of the things I see in the second half of the book is that he starts to really punish her. It’s like he doesn’t know what to do with her, really. He starts being really mean about her physical appearance, which I get is a manifestation of her evil. But because he’s filled with empathy and understanding for her by this point in the book, it felt to me a little bit underdeveloped. I was curious about: What’s the more fully embodied version of what happens to Cathy? Why does she kill herself? How do we get there?

	One of the things that really struck me was that this character is operating from the viewpoint that the world is full of folly and evil. This is a person who’s really isolated herself, who has run from love, who has thought of love as a trap, and who has done everything in her power not to be trapped. And here she is in her 30s, and she has no one she can trust because of how she’s built her life. In the book, she builds a little gray room with no windows that she can go in and close the door. For budget reasons, I had to not have her build this little room, but I tried to turn her whole bedroom into that room for herself. I thought about a world in which this person is carrying trauma and has had no access to anyone helping her with her mental health. I was also thinking about the morphine use that is implied in the story — she carries this little bottle of morphine around her neck — and I stepped off from there.



	

									Courtesy of KIRSTY GRIFFIN/NETFLIX
	




	
		Cathy starts losing her mind in Episode 6, when she begins to hear Charles’ voice in her head. What do you think is the significance of him haunting her towards the end of her life?	

	The tools of a novelist are totally different than the tools of a dramatist. As a novelist, you can just tell us what she’s thinking about. When you’re trying to put it on film, voiceover is an option. But other than that, you need to give characters someone to talk to. There’s a chapter in this book where she’s walking through her house at night, and she starts to imagine that Charles is with her. She starts to feel that he’s watching her, and she thinks to herself, “He’s maybe the only person I could have loved.” It really struck me as this very strange and youthful idea.

	I was riffing off of this thought about “Alice in Wonderland” and her having this imaginary friend, and I thought, “OK, well, I can give her this imaginary friend in Charles.” I had thought of her voiceover from the top of the show as being her talking to herself, and I thought, “I wonder if I can use Charles as a conduit for her talking to herself.” And then she starts to have to confront the fact that she’s not actually talking to Charles, but rather she’s been talking to herself.



	

					Christopher Abbott and Hoon Lee 
									Courtesy of Netflix
	




	
		You originally wrote eight episodes, but you were reportedly only able to make seven episodes for budgetary reasons. The episode you unfortunately had to cut centered around Lee’s trip to San Francisco, and you had to reduce that storyline to only a handful of scenes.	

	No matter how many resources we were given, I can’t imagine a number that would’ve been enough for us to do all the things that we originally wanted to do. It’s just a very ambitious project — so many locations, so many actors, spanning over 50 years, it’s period. There’s a lot that made this very expensive. So I cut about 10 pages out of every episode, and then on top of that, it became clear that we did not have the budget to build San Francisco in 1912. Because it was a standalone episode, there were so many locations that we were never going to use again, and it would’ve scaled up our budget by a third.


	
		One of the biggest unanswered questions of Steinbeck’s novel is what happened to Lee in San Francisco. Your version shows that he left the Trasks to pursue his long-held dream of opening a bookstore, but the societal barriers and hardships — including racism — he experienced made him realize that his true home was with the Trask men. For that storyline, how did you settle on what actually made it into the final cut?	

	There’s so many things about Steinbeck’s portrayal of Lee that are so humanist, and then there are moments in the book where I feel like the racism of the time period in which he was writing really came through. His seeming lack of curiosity about what happened to Lee in San Francisco felt to me like the product of mid-century white America. I thought, “I’m going to hire an Asian American writer to imagine this with me.” I had just read Alexander Chee’s book, “Edinburgh,” which I highly recommend. That book portrays a really lonely character. I saw some correlation between that character and Lee, and I thought, “OK, he’s the right person. I’ll put a novelist’s imagination on this. We’ll figure this out together.” He had never really written a script before, so I knew I would end up writing it with him.

	Once I knew I was going to have to cut that episode out, what it really boiled down to me was that it was important that all of our protagonists have a journey that is somewhere in relation to this idea of timshel and this idea of choosing. I wanted to know more about Lee’s choice to abandon his dream of this bookstore, and even more importantly, his choice to come back and really become a parent to these children. Once I used that as a rubric, then some of the plot that Alex had invented and some of the themes that I had written just seemed less important. I was like, “We can let go of those things.” But lines that felt really important remained — like this line that Alex wrote, “It sounds like you were someone else’s imaginary wife.”

	I truly believe that Lee’s storyline is stronger for being integrated with the rest of this story and not siloed into its own episode. I thought more deeply about how he is woven into the fabric of the story. I just want to say that the person that I really tip my hat to in all of this is Hoon Lee, who came in with so many questions, so much of his own lived experience. If we have done our job of giving Lee a bigger life here, it is really because of the gentle and confident hands that this role was in.



	

									Courtesy of Netflix
	




	
		I heard through the grapevine that you and Alex chose to make Lee gay in this adaptation, although his sexuality isn’t actually addressed in the final cut. Is that true?	

	When I read the book, I ask myself that question about Lee’s sexuality — and I ask it with a lot of trepidation because I know Asian American men in Western media have a history with a lot of damaging feminization, and I don’t want to participate in that. But I think that this sort of “platonic marriage” that he and Adam are in is fascinating. There are things about this character that I feel like are very private, even from its author. I asked myself those questions, and I brought those questions to Alex. That said, I don’t presume to know what Hoon was thinking — I never talked to Hoon about that — and none of those discussions that Alex and I had made it into the finished product.


	
		The devastating climax of the story occurs when Cal Trask (Joseph Zada) takes his idealist twin Aron (Joe Anders) to see their mother’s brothel, driving Aron to join the army and then get killed in WWI. Lee convinces Adam to give Cal his blessing on Adam’s deathbed, essentially absolving Cal of the lifelong guilt that he will feel over his brother’s death. What was your approach to writing that final scene, and where do you think we leave the surviving characters after the screen cuts to black?	

	What’s in the book created such a clear map. Man, Steinbeck really killed it with that last scene. I knew that I was writing towards that the whole time. Knowing that that scene was coming actually was a North Star for me in how I wrote the rest of the series: “I know I need to have Samuel Hamilton and Lee tell the story of Cain and Abel, so how do I make that palatable to a contemporary audience?”

	I don’t know where we leave them. Steinbeck’s original conception of the book would’ve gone through another generation. I, for one, don’t know if I could have taken another tragic Trask generation of men, so I’m glad he decided to cut it off where he did. One of the beautiful things about books that sing across time is that these characters can feel so real to so many of us. There are certain scenes in this show — like the scene where Cathy gets beat up by Mr. Edwards, or the last scene of the series where Lee asks Adam to give his son his blessing — that I wrote once and basically never touched again, because they were so upsetting to write and think about deeply.



	

					Joseph Zada
									Courtesy of Netflix
	




	
		You and Jeb Stuart are reteaming with Netflix on an adaptation of “Lonesome Dove.” What kind of prior relationship did you have with that book prior to signing on to adapt it, and what intrigues you about the prospect of reimagining that story for a contemporary audience?	

	I couldn’t have a more different relationship with this book, and that feels like a relief. This has been six years of my life, but it was a good 20 years of thinking about this book before that. I don’t know that I could have bled out for another series, at least not right now.

	I had never read any Larry McMurtry. We would be standing around on set at two in the morning trying to stay awake, and Jeb would talk to me about his love for Larry McMurtry and “Lonesome Dove” and why I should read it. I felt like, “That looks like a book for boys. That’s not for me.” And when I got back to the States [from New Zealand], I started reading “Lonesome Dove,” and it totally blew my mind. I think like all great Westerns, it’s a rumination on death and how we make meaning of our lives in the face of our certain mortality. I’m also just really drawn to these stories of a moment in time when everything is changing, the way that it was at the turn of the century here, and the way that it was in the West in the 1870s.

	The process of getting to know this book has been totally joyful. The original miniseries is incredible, obviously, and I don’t think anyone would presume that we are going to do better than Robert Duvall as Gus. That’s a performance for the ages. But I do think that these stories can be told again and again by different people. There’s so much that was unexplored in that version of the miniseries. Every reader comes to a book with their own life experience, and between Jeb and me, we have a lot of really interesting life experience to bring to bear here.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘East of Eden’ Boss Zoe Kazan on That Devastating Ending, Why Florence Pugh’s Cathy Is Both a ‘Murderer’ and ‘Survivor’ and Making Lee a Central Character

title: Daily Wire’s Pro-ICE Film ‘Pawn Shop’ Production Temporarily Suspended
description: Production of Daily Wire’s pro-ICE film “Pawn Shop” has been temporarily halted in Livingston, Mont., following a Special City Commission Meeting he
body:
Production of Daily Wire’s pro-ICE film “Pawn Shop” has been temporarily halted in Livingston, Mont., following a Special City Commission Meeting held on Saturday.

	The action comes as Livingston locals raised concerns about the film’s impact on local business — and notably the city’s sole food bank — as well as improper notification about hazardous stunts. During the meeting, residents voiced worries about the filming, saying it made them feel unsafe. City Commission member Cindy Daniels explained that she felt that “they’ve taken advantage of the situation to make their movie… We’re not profiting off that movie. So they’re not thinking of the veterans that live on K Street. They’re not thinking of the food resource center.”
	

	The Livingston Commission concluded: “A motion to immediately temporarily suspend Bonfire Pawn Shop LLC’s permit while seeking legal opinion from the city attorney in a timely manner to amend, suspend, or revoke the permit to come back to the commission not after 5:00pm on October 5th.”


	Daily Wire did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment.

	The halting of filming comes days after locals in Livingston protested against the film’s production, which has been reported to include an opening scene depicting the fatal ICE shooting of Renée Good that occurred in Minnesota earlier this year.

	The Livingston Food Resource Center posted a statement on Instagram on Friday, explaining how filming “Pawn Shop” has affected its clients. 

	“People who already face numerous obstacles to meeting their most basic needs are not facing additional completely avoidable barriers to accessing food because of how this production was permitted,” it read. “We were not notified of the plans to film,” the statement continued, noting that attendance at the pantry was down 17% on Tuesday, “an eight-week low from seeing 90-100+ households a day. That is unacceptable.”

title: ‘Spotlight’ Director Says The Catholic Church Hasn’t Done ‘Enough’ To Protect Children From Sexual Assault 10 Years After Film’s Best Picture Win: ‘Not Until Every Child Is Safe’
description: Tom McCarthy’s biographical drama “Spotlight” won Best Picture at the Academy Awards in 2016. The film, featuring a stacked ensemble led by Michael
body:
Tom McCarthy’s biographical drama “Spotlight” won Best Picture at the Academy Awards in 2016. The film, featuring a stacked ensemble led by Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams and Mark Ruffalo, was widely praised for chronicling the investigative reporting by the Boston Globe that exposed the Catholic Church’s systemic cover-up of sexual abuse of children by priests. A decade later, McCarthy says his influential film still hasn’t galvanized enough change within the church.
	

	“I’ve heard from a lot of people who saw the movie. A lot of people who felt understood after the movie was released,” McCarthy told Variety Saturday night at the New York Film Festival. “Has it caused a lot of change within the Catholic Church? In my opinion, not really. Not enough. It’s not enough until every child is safe, as far as I’m concerned. And that’s a zero sum game. So, I would like to see more change.”


	McCarthy’s new film, “A Statement,” could be seen as a cathartic response to the lack of institutional change that followed “Spotlight.” Bolstered by a strong ensemble led by Paul Rudd, the film follows 20 experts who attempt to reach a consensus on a statement to Congress about the effects of carbon dioxide emissions on the climate.

	Based on a real-life conference that took place in St. Petersburg, Fla., in 1980, the film’s opening text calls the gathering “the first meeting dedicated to solving the climate crisis in America.” The group, ultimately, never reached a consensus — and nearly 50 years later, the debate over carbon emissions continues to divide American politics.
	

	“I’m very proud of [‘Spotlight’],” McCarthy explained. “I think, as filmmakers, our job is to start a conversation, get people thinking about an issue, but draw a light on things. That’s what I think we’ve done with ‘Spotlight,’ and hopefully, we’ve done that with ‘A Statement.’ This movie doesn’t preach. There is a right and wrong here, but we want people to come to the table and have thaat conversation and listen.”

	Coincidentally, “A Statement” premiered the same weekend Tom Cruise’s “Digger” bombed at the box office. Variety’s Owen Gleiberman panned the film as a “bombastically self-important satire” that attempts to be “the ‘Dr. Strangelove’ of climate change.” Nathaniel Rich, who wrote the 2019 nonfiction book “Losing Earth” that McCarthy based his script on, used the same adjective when describing “A Statement.” At the festival, he called McCarthy’s film the “first climate change movie written for adults” and praised it for being “not bombastic.”

	“I haven’t seen [‘Digger] but I’m very curious to see it,” Rich said. “All I can say is there has not been a film like [‘A Statement’] before. There are some films like this on other social justice issues that movie beyond a kind of polemic into a deeper exploration of the material. That hasn’t happened with climate change in a feature film until now.”On Thursday, 21 states sued the Trump administration over its repeal of federal greenhouse gas regulations for power plants. While the Trump-led EPA believes that eliminating the Biden-era limits will lower costs and boost American energy production, the Democratic-led coalition argues the rollback will set the country back decades in its fight against climate change. The back-and-forth is the latest example of how climate action, nearly half a century after the meeting depicted in “A Statement,” has become poisoned by partisan politics.

	“Everything becomes politicized,” Rudd said. “This was not a politicized issue. This [gathering] was really smart people, Republicans and Democrats alike, who realized, ‘Oh, this is an existential threat and it is something that we should deal with. Now, how we go about dealing with it, we need to figure that out — but the science is there. We know.’”

	But do we know? At the end of the film, Paul Giamatti’s David Slade (a government director at the Department of Energy) offers a reassuring one-liner to Tatiana Maslany’s character about the factual nature of science. The 1980 gathering took place just four days before Ronald Reagan won the presidency.
	

	“Presidents come and go,” Slade said, “but if there’s one thing we’ll always agree on, it’s science.”

	“Yeah, well,” Rudd laughed. “I think he said that with a bit of a wink.”

schema.headline: ‘Spotlight’ Director Says The Catholic Church Hasn’t Done ‘Enough’ To Protect Children From Sexual Assault 10 Years After Film’s Best Picture Win: ‘Not Until Every Child Is Safe’

title: Pedro Pascal in ‘Behemoth!’: The Oscar-Worthy Role That He (and Latinos) Have Been Waiting For
description:
Pedro Pascal makes his Oscar case with a cello.

	“Behemoth!,” Tony Gilroy’s first feature as a director since “The Bourne Legacy” in 2012, world-pr
body:
Pedro Pascal makes his Oscar case with a cello.

	“Behemoth!,” Tony Gilroy’s first feature as a director since “The Bourne Legacy” in 2012, world-premiered on Friday night at Alice Tully Hall as the centerpiece selection of the New York Film Festival. Pascal plays Alex Serian, a former child prodigy from a family of Los Angeles studio musicians who returns home after 20 years on tour to record Hollywood film scores.


	Pascal offers a beautiful, internalized performance that ranks among his best work on film. More than that, it’s the first time a director has built a movie on the merit of what happens across Pascal’s face when nobody is talking.
	

	Pascal did not get his fame from the movies. He was almost 40 when his “Game of Thrones” character Oberyn Martell became one of the most beloved — and most egregiously short-lived — characters In TV history.  Then came more series work on “Narcos,” “The Mandalorian” and “The Last of Us.” On that ascent, Pascal became an internet boyfriend (“Daddy,” as many have called him). You can’t blame me for worrying about audiences focusing on his depth and talent amid the thirst. 

	It is, perhaps, why his scene-stealing performance in the 2022 action-comedy “The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent” went suspiciously ignored. He played Javi, the billionaire superfan of Nicolas Cage (and maybe a cartel kingpin), who went toe-to-toe with one of the most gloriously unhinged actors of his generation. Pascal stole every frame. 

	Pedro Almodóvar’s short “Strange Way of Life,” Celine Song’s “Materialists” and Ari Aster’s “Eddington” gave Pascal latitude. Gilroy and “Behemoth!” make him undeniable. 
	



	

					Pedro Pascal in “Behemoth!”
									Courtesy of Searchlight Pictures
	



	Gilroy structures the movie around flashbacks. Each time Pascal’s Alex sits down to play the opening cue of a different movie score, the music sends him back to the people and circumstances that made him flee. Pascal doesn’t overtly articulate those memories. We feel them in looks, pauses and slight changes in his posture. The performance rises in those moments.

	Pascal’s work recalls Jude Law in “Cold Mountain,” which is still my go-to example of a reserved performance surviving an Oscar season that typically rewards outsized performances. In that film, Law’s wounded soldier Inman barely speaks during his long walk home from the Civil War, yet voters noticed him anyway. There isn’t a war for Pascal to walk through unless you count the one in his mind —  concerning his father (Hank Azaria) or his brother (Will Arnett). 

	And then there’s Olivia Wilde. Somehow, her knockout year directing and starring in “The Invite,” and reminding us all of her command and delicious appeal in “I Want Your Sex,” gets better. She devours every frame in “Behemoth!” as the ex Pascal can’t quite shake. She’s channeling a little Cameron Diaz in “Vanilla Sky,” harboring obsession with a scary fuse. Noteworthy: Diaz received a Golden Globe and a SAG nomination for that performance, but the Academy passed. This doesn’t deserve that same fate.

	Nonetheless, the real star of “Behemoth!” is the music itself.

	Gilroy recruited nine composers, each scoring a different fictional film within the film. The result is a soundtrack that moves across eras and genres in the same way Alex’s memory does. The team includes Michael Abels (“Get Out”) along with pianist and composer Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Michael Giacchino (“Up”), James Newton Howard (“Michael Clayton”), Henry Jackman (“Captain America: The Winter Soldier”), Nami Melumad (Pixar’s “Dream Productions”), Brandon Roberts (“Andor”) and Alan Silvestri (“Forrest Gump”).

	There’s a bit of irony for anyone who follows the score race. Giacchino already has the statuette, winning for “Up” in 2010. James Newton Howard, who scored Gilroy’s “Michael Clayton,” is one of the Academy’s great bridesmaids, with multiple nominations and no wins. Silvestri, whose noms and credits include “Forrest Gump” and “Back to the Future,” has never won either.
	

	The title refers to the giant fake movie the story builds toward. Gilroy created a tribute to the Los Angeles scoring community he believes is disappearing. Following the film academy’s 2024 rule change, as many as three composers can receive individual statuettes for original score. However, nine still don’t fit, unless they enter as a “group” and share the nom (meaning a lone Oscar statuette). A movie about musicians, ironically, could be shut out or disqualified from the category built for them, if the music branch chooses ego over artistic merit.

	Admittedly, the film won’t be for everyone. “Behemoth!” is very “Tár”-coded. It focuses on a protagonist whose gift and damage come from the same place. Some will find the fake-movie conceit too clever, and others may think the climax goes too small.

	Underneath it all is a simple, aching idea about love and what we think we’re entitled to. That’s Gilroy’s brilliant screenplay at work.

	“Behemoth!” premiered in the middle of Hispanic Heritage Month, and for the Latinos who have been rooting for Pascal since Oberyn, this has been a long time coming.

	Look at who came before him.

	José Ferrer, a Puerto Rican, won for “Cyrano de Bergerac” and became the first Latino actor to take home a best actor Oscar. Seventy-five years later, he is still the only one. Mexican Anthony Quinn, who won two supporting Oscars, received lead nominations for “Wild Is the Wind” and “Zorba the Greek” but never took home the top prize. Then came Edward James Olmos for “Stand and Deliver,” Demián Bichir for “A Better Life,” Colman Domingo for “Rustin” and “Sing Sing” and most recently, Wagner Moura, who last season became the first Brazilian ever nominated in the category, for “The Secret Agent.”

	And Pascal may not be the only Latino celebrating at the upcoming 99th Academy Awards.

	John Leguizamo, who received the Career Achievement Award at the Critics Choice Celebracion ceremony the same day as the “Behemoth” premiere, has been grinding for four decades. As Eumaeus, the swineherd who remains loyal, he’s the heartbeat of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey.” He has never been nominated for an Oscar but that also looks to change this year.

	We must sit still and hold the note for Pedro.
	

	“Behemoth!” opens on Dec 4.

schema.headline: Pedro Pascal in ‘Behemoth!’: The Oscar-Worthy Role That He (and Latinos) Have Been Waiting For
